articles.title: Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunion
articles.summary: The Gallagher brothers’ comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created. “Hello … hello … It’s good to be back.” With these words – and the unfortunate possibility of a royalty payment to a certain disgraced ex-pop star …
body: Yet to the surprise of many who did not believe, and these biblical echoes are strangely appropriate, Liam and Noel did not fall out; the resulting stadium tour put a fresh coat of paint on the word “phenomenon”. Middle-aged and elderly people together with young people sporting bucket hats, some accompanied by their pets in bucket hats, sang their hearts out as if it was the 90s again and Manchester City had just won the World Cup 10-0 (although this film was evidently completed before Wonderwall’s moment at this year’s World Cup ).

As for the brothers’ togetherness, I think the film shows it is sincere and real in public, and real on stage, where it counts. Noel and Liam are rarely interviewed together; here mostly it is Noel solo. I wonder if, like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, they now come together to make music after reaching an accommodation. Whatever wound each other up has not magically vanished, but is being managed. Part of the problem was that Noel’s songwriting credits made the big money – not Liam. Perhaps the lawyers have hammered something out here, but it is not shown in the film.

articles.title: ‘Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger’ Review: An Uncharacteristically Polite and Sentimental Portrait of a Raucous Band and Phenomenon
articles.summary: The 2016 documentary “Supersonic,” focused on Oasis’ beginnings and incredibly fast rise to superstardom, made no mention of what was then the most salient fact about the Gallagher brothers: that from 2009, they were no longer on speaking terms.
body: Shot during the Mancunian band’s 2025 reunion tour, Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace's documentary features impressive concert footage interrupted by clumsy attempts at earnestness.

Although neither Noel nor Liam can help expressing themselves, in new on-camera interviews, in the candid manner that they always have, they remain not just on their best behavior, but also at what feels like a PR-trained remove. Their professional focus — the usually raucous Liam is described by a band member as being uncharacteristically “business” in rehearsals — is in step with a film whose attempts to conceal its obvious financial raison d’etre often feel absurd and tacked-on.

articles.title: Hey, Oscars: No Sympathy Required to Give Mike Leigh’s ‘Tender Loving Care’ the Consideration It Deserves
articles.summary: Let’s dispense with the suspense. Mike Leigh has been nominated for an Academy Award seven times and has won it zero times. That seems wrong. He has a Palme d’Or, a Golden Lion, five decades of films that taught generations of actors what unglamorous truth looks like and one of the most distinctive…
body: That makes the season’s obvious question unavoidable: What should the Academy do with Mike Leigh’s final film? The answer is not — give him an Oscar because he is 83.

“Tender Loving Care” does not need a sympathy campaign. It is vintage Leigh — wry, melancholy, humane, alert to the small emotional humiliations that become, over the course of a life, the events that define us. Kate O’Flynn’s Amy anchors it — an Emmy nominee for “Widow’s Bay,” and when the trophies are handed out Sept. 14, very possibly a winner — a social worker steadying a father in decline, gutted by a breakup and kept upright by wine and by Rosie, the live-wire best friend played exquisitely by Alice Bailey Johnson. Marion Bailey, as Amy’s mother, has already emerged from Telluride as a standout, a veteran thespian never given her proper due.

articles.title: ‘Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes’ Review: The Legendary Rocker Gets a Lively Doc That Asks: Who Are You? And Then Doesn’t Fully Answer It
articles.summary: The film centers itself on Pete Townshend’s contradictions, his growing pains, his turmoil, and his complexity as a human being and rock artist. And that’s all good. But given where it sets the bar, there’s too much that's left out.
body: The film includes a lot of great footage of the Who, but it's most interested in Townshend's anguished moody poetic side.

Every rock god has his ultimate gesture of power, and for Pete Townshend it was not the way he liked to smash his guitar (though that came close). No, the quintessential Townshend power sign was his giant circular windmill strum, arm outstretched and twirling, gathering centrifugal force to slam that pick up through the guitar strings, creating the loudest chord humanly possible.

It’s strange, though, that “Behind Blue Eyes” skips over the epochal moment of “My Generation,” one of the 10 most seismic and influential songs in the history of rock ‘n’ roll. When punk finally came along, the movie talks about how Townshend, who totally dug the punk scene, tried to cozy up to Johnny Rotten and got nowhere. It notes how much influence the Who had on punk — but that would be “My Generation,” which the film never got around to mentioning!
points: The film centers itself on Pete Townshend’s contradictions, his growing pains, his turmoil, and his complexity as a human being and rock artist.
But given where it sets the bar, there’s too much that's left out.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson says he had ‘twice as much time’ after birth of first child
articles.summary: Actor says of busy 2026 in which he has had several big roles: ‘Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive’ Robert Pattinson has talked about the “addictive” nature of working on several films simultaneously, having starred in several of this year’s most highly anticipated productions…
body: “Once you get the momentum going, it’s strangely not that hard,” said Pattinson at the Venice film festival. “Once you start spinning plates, it gets quite addictive.”

The London-born performer has drawn critical praise this year for his turn as Antinous, the primary antagonist in Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, as well as playing a lead role in the dark romantic comedy The Drama and making his Dune debut in the third instalment of the franchise this December.

On the Venice Lido, Pattinson was promoting Lance Oppenheim’s forthcoming arthouse thriller Primetime, which he joined as a producer before agreeing to star as the lead, and prepared while filming Lynne Ramsay’s Die My Love with Jennifer Lawrence.
“I just had a baby,” the actor told a press conference on the Lido. “So I had no desire to go out at night, so suddenly I had twice as much time to do anything with, which was very helpful.”

articles.title: Andrew Scott Has Waited His Whole Career for a Role Like ‘Elsinore.’ Can Focus and the Bard Anoint Him With an Oscar?
articles.summary: Andrew Scott is the prince of Telluride. There are performances that feel like a reckoning, and performances that feel like a resurrection. Andrew Scott’s work in “Elsinore,” which had its world premiere Friday night at the Telluride Film Festival, is somehow both — a great actor playing a great…
body: Make no mistake, this is the role of Scott’s career and it lands him toward the forefront of a best actor conversation he has been circling for years. He has never been Oscar-nominated — a fact that curdled into open disdain when the Academy passed over his shattering turn in “All of Us Strangers.” “Elsinore” is the correction: he captures Charleson’s wit, vanity, terror and grace inside the same breath and in the final stretch, he nails Hamlet’s readiness measured against a dying man’s own — the sustained high-wire work voters still see behind their eyes in January.

It’s also a role the Academy has never resisted. Voters are reliably moved by the actor staring down the barrel of death — Tom Hanks in “Philadelphia” (1993), Matthew McConaughey in “Dallas Buyers Club” (2013) and Anthony Hopkins vanishing into dementia in “The Father” (2020).

articles.title: ‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxes
articles.summary: The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram. In outsider visionaries such as Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo or Timothy Treadwell, renegade German director Werner Herzog has created some of cinema’s most memorable monomaniacs – characters…
body: But suggestions that they could be role models for the modern-day neurodiversity movement send this famously fearless film-maker running for the hills. “I don’t like the term neurodivergence and ADHD, or whatever – it sounds like political correctness, which scares me under the table,” Herzog said at the Venice film festival.

The protagonist pair of Bucking Fastard, the new film that Herzog has brought to the Lido, slots right into his gallery of single-minded outsiders. Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara play siblings Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who have separate bodies but speak in unison, dress the same and share the same preoccupations.

First they fall in love with their washed-up heart-throb neighbour (played by Orlando Bloom) and exact revenge when he marries another woman, then they embark on a quixotic quest to dig a tunnel connecting a cave in County Sligo to the Orkneys. Contemporary psychiatrists might detect behaviour consistent with autism or ADHD hyper-focus. Not Herzog.

articles.summary: "We couldn't raise the money," the film's Oscar-winning director reveals. "A lot of people thought theater plays don't really work in film, and they were all frightened of Murdoch and legal problems."
body: Hot on the heels of Wednesday evening’s Venice Film Festival world premiere of Ink, a film about the relationship between businessman Rupert Murdoch and newspaperman Larry Lamb on London’s Fleet Street back in the 1960s, the film’s director Danny Boyle, writer James Graham and star Jack O’Connell (who plays Lamb opposite Guy Pearce’s Murdoch) flew in to Telluride for the film’s North American premiere on Friday — and granted their first joint interview to The Hollywood Reporter.
Congratulations on the film’s great reception in Venice — and on opening night, no less!

articles.title: Gilligan's Island Star Tina Louise Headlined A Bleak '50s Western That Every Genre Fan Has To Watch
articles.summary: Tina Louise, best known for playing Ginger on Gilligan's Island, was in a spectacular and unconventional Western a few years before joining the show.
body: The 1950s and 60s were the era of the classic TV Western and a last hurrah for the traditional Western movie prior to the revisionist era's arrival. As such, if you were a working actor at the time, chances are your filmography was filled with Old West adventures. That was certainly the case for "Gilligan's Island" star Tina Louise, who, prior to playing Ginger Grant on the beloved CBS sitcom, teamed up with Robert Ryan and Burl Ives for the grim Western "Day of the Outlaw."

By the end of the 50s, then, de Toth was a well-established Hollywood director with several classics to his name. With "Day of the Outlaw," he delivered one of his most interesting and most underrated Westerns: A film he described (via TCM ) as "a story of tension and fear, survival in a prison of snow." As such, after Tina Louise was cast as the love interest and arrived in Oregon for filming, she found herself about as far from the secluded tropical environs of Gilligan's Isle as she could possible get.

articles.title: Johnny Flynn and Aimee Lou Wood on “Getting Whipped Naked” and “Embracing the Madness” of Their Deranged Literary Biopic
articles.summary: 'The Idiot(s),' which premiered Friday night in Telluride, is unlike anything else on the fall circuit: “There'd be days where they would say…‘Today you're going to be shitting on your landlady's doorstep.’”
body: What went into one of the wildest works from one of our greatest literary minds? The Idiot(s) cannot be fully trusted on matters of factual accuracy, but in the unhinged spirit of its portrait of the love between Fyodor Dostoevsky ( Johnny Flynn ) and his great love of the time, Anna ( Aimee Lou Wood ) — set during the period when the former went on to write his novel The Idiot — you can trust that the filmmakers and artists had their own kind of singular, bizarre creative alchemy going.
This is a highly idiosyncratic project from two Polish filmmakers. How did you get involved?

AIMEE LOU WOOD I met Małgo on Zoom and she told me that she had the perfect part for me. We spoke about the film for about five minutes and then for two hours or something we just spoke about astrology, our whole life stories, everything. We just went completely off. It was not a conventional kind of meeting. And we just loved each other so much. The movie was always changing and shifting, including when we were filming it. There was a lot of off-the-cuff stuff.
